title: 393. The most dangerous person in a brainstorm
author: The Best Leadership Newsletter
summary: The author, a consultant who is paid by large brands to join their brainstorms, argues that he is in the room not to supply ideas but to fix the room. He traces the brainstorm to Alex Osborn and notes that research shows group brainstorming yields fewer and weaker ideas than people working alone and then pooling results. Two causes are production blocking, where ideas are forgotten or abandoned while waiting for a turn, and status effects, where senior voices dominate and their ideas are overweighted. His two antidotes are to ask sharper questions and give everyone quiet individual time to write answers first, and to watch for the silent people whose ideas are hiding. A story about a quiet CTO whose six-word suggestion led to an acquisition illustrates the point. For leaders, the most dangerous move is to speak first, because the boss's idea becomes a magnet; the advice is to talk last.
points: Group brainstorming underperforms individual ideation followed by pooling because of production blocking and status effects, so the room's design is the problem rather than the people's creativity.
Opening with a provocative question and giving everyone silent time to write individually lets ideas form before group influence sets in.
The person talking the most is rarely the one worth hearing, so facilitators should watch quiet participants and invite them in, sometimes twice.
A silent CTO's six-word acquisition idea shows that good ideas are often already in the room waiting to be heard.
Senior leaders who share their idea early turn it into a magnet, so the practical rule is to speak last or leave the room.
quotes: I'm not in the room to come up with ideas. I'm in the room to fix the room.
Research continues to prove that group brainstorming doesn’t work. It produces fewer ideas, and lower-quality ones, than if the same people worked alone and then pooled their results.

Because as you’re listening to others speak, your idea just sits there. Maybe you forget what it is before you even say it. Or the conversation moves on and it just doesn’t feel right to share anymore.
In the 1970s, sociologists found that the people in the room with the most status do the most talking. Fifty years later, it still happens. They’re still talking.
Because the best way to get more ideas out of a room is to stop making everyone compete for the opportunity to share them.
The person doing the most talking is rarely the person I’m most interested in hearing. I’m looking at the people who aren’t talking.

It didn’t need to be invented. It just needed to be heard. That’s what happens in brainstorms. It convinces some people their ideas are more important and makes others believe that their ideas aren’t worth sharing.
The moment you share your ideas, it becomes a magnet. Suddenly the entire room is brainstorming ways to make your idea work
And if you’re the most senior person in the room, talk last. Or get the hell out of the room.
